passage: Rain kept the boys indoors, and toys lay everywhere in Abebe's room. Abebe's aunt said they could have a story once the floor was clear. Emeka groaned and lay flat on the rug. Abebe thought, then held up one finger. "I do the cars, you do the books, then we read a story." "Deal," said Emeka, sitting up. Abebe rolled the cars into a crate and counted them aloud. Emeka stacked the books on the low shelf. When they finished, they flopped down and opened the book about the tortoise.

qa.a: Abebe said, "I do the cars, you do the books, then we read a story."

qa.q: How did Emeka feel about clearing up at the start, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Emeka felt reluctant. Emeka groaned and lay flat on the rug.

qa.q: What other approach could work if Emeka had refused the deal, and why?
qa.a: Abebe could turn the clearing into a race or a shop game. Play can make a chore feel lighter.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Emeka?
qa.a: Emeka gets a clear, fair share of the work and a story to look forward to. That is why sitting up and saying "Deal" makes sense.

grounding: A child splits the tidying between two children and names a story as the reward.
